summary:
Cuba's constitutional and statutory framework is unusually explicit. Article 42 of the 2019 Constitution names sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories, the first constitution to do so, and the Family Code approved by referendum on 25 September 2022 with 66.87% support legalised same-sex marriage and adoption and provides for legal gender change without surgery. Consensual same-sex relations were struck from the Penal Code in 1979.

Legal gender recognition runs through the civil registry rather than a court or a medical gate. The Family Code establishes that surgery is not a precondition, and the July 2025 civil-registry reform removed the remaining administrative hurdles to name changes.

Employment protection stops short of the constitutional wording. A labor-law amendment approved by lawmakers in December 2013 banned employment discrimination on sexual orientation after extended parliamentary debate. The Labor Code (Law 116) bars discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation, but article 2(b) covers orientation and does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground. CENESEX, the state body for sexual diversity, had proposed extending the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status; the sexual-orientation ban is the confirmed outcome of that legislative effort.

Trans healthcare is inside the public system. Resolution 126 brought gender-related care into state health provision in 2008, and CENESEX has run a sustained state-backed programme including trans-rights campaigning, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education in schools. Official institutions have campaigned for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s, and Fidel Castro publicly accepted blame for the UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men in 2010.

The equality settlement is contested rather than uniformly enforced. Opponents of the 2022 Family Code cited religious objections and argued that child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July 2021 crackdown. A visitor should expect legal protection on paper alongside uneven application in daily life.

The historical baseline matters for context. UMAP camps operated from 1965 to 1968 in Camagüey, where conscripts performed roughly 60 hours a week of cane cutting for seven pesos a day and were subjected to electric-shock and injection experiments presented as 'curing'. A 1975 declaration-era shift and the 1979 Penal Code change mark the turn toward the present framework.
tangentialFactors:
Cuba's hostility in the sources is directed at emigration rather than at gender expression. In January 2018, Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres filed asylum claims in the Netherlands and faced charges of 'treason against the homeland' carrying up to eight years in prison if they returned; a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018, and LGBTI activists including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation remained under monitoring.

The political environment around the equality legislation is unsettled. The September 2022 referendum was only the fourth national vote since 1959, and the count followed the July 2021 unrest in which more than 1,400 people were arrested amid record emigration.

The 2013 employment amendment predates both the 2019 Constitution and the 2022 Family Code, so the statutory layer and the constitutional layer were built at different moments and do not yet align on gender identity.
localsOnly:
Residents can marry and adopt on the same terms regardless of sex under the 2022 Family Code, which also codifies penalties for domestic violence and shared parental rights and provides for surrogacy.

CENESEX operates as the state-facing point of contact for sexual-diversity education and trans-rights advocacy, with an established working relationship with the police and the supreme court.

Workplace complaints on the ground of sexual orientation fall under the Labor Code as amended in 2013; a discrimination claim framed specifically on gender identity lacks an equivalent express statutory ground in article 2(b).

Name changes are handled administratively through the civil registry, without a surgical or judicial requirement.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory reviewed for this pass contains no sourced information on restroom or facility access, on the marker wording available on Cuban identity documents, on entry or visa screening of transgender travellers, on hate-crime provisions, or on recognition of a foreign spouse or partner. These are unresolved and are not stated either way here.

Whether the July 2025 civil-registry reform is applied uniformly across all municipal registries is not documented in the sources reviewed.

The current status of the proposed gender-identity extension to the Labor Code, first put forward by CENESEX during the 2013 debates, is unresolved: the inventory confirms the sexual-orientation ban only.

Enforcement data on how often the constitutional or Family Code protections are invoked in practice, and whether any court has applied Article 42 to a gender-identity claim, is not sourced here.

No figures are available on reported violence against trans people in Cuba, including any incidents during the period of the 2021 crackdown.
